opus-5.5.text:
Ha, I think Ken was being only half-joking. When the Putnam came out, we had a very short window. The problems are released, and suddenly the question is whether our system can produce fully verified Lean proofs, not just plausible-looking answers, in a matter of hours. That's a very different bar from "the model got the right number at the end."

So for those few days the whole team was in that mode. People were sleeping in shifts, watching the prover run, catching infrastructure issues at three in the morning, checking which problems had closed and which were still stuck. Nobody was hand-writing proofs. The point was that the system had to do it on its own. But everything around it, the compute, the pipelines, the formalization of the problem statements, had to be correct and had to hold up under pressure.

Ken has been around competition math his whole life. He's mentored a lot of strong students, so he knows what the Putnam means to people. I think seeing a young team treat it with that intensity, like everything was on the line, reminded him of a war room. And honestly, for a startup, it kind of was. It was our first big public test of whether formal verification plus AI reasoning could work in the real world on problems nobody had seen before.

For me, that was the most meaningful part. It wasn't about the score. Every proof that came out was checked by Lean, so there was no ambiguity and no grader being generous. Either it's proven or it isn't. That kind of certainty is what we think mathematical AI needs. So "wartime" captures the stress, but it also captures how focused everyone was on one clear goal.

r001.rationale: The response describes a short deadline after the problems were released, but does not say the morning paper alone had more problems to solve than expected across both sessions.

r002.rationale: It mentions team members monitoring the prover, but does not identify near-exclusive dependence on Evan Chen as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It contrasts verified proofs with plausible answers, but does not distinguish research mathematics from competition mathematics under severe time constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "wartime" was Ken's way of describing the pace more than anything else. We had a hard deadline that we did not set. The Putnam happens on one Saturday in December, and the problems are only released that morning. So there was no way to push the date, and there was no way to prepare for the specific questions. Everything had to be ready before we knew what we were facing.

That changes how a team works. In normal research, you can take a week to think about one lemma. Here, we were asking: does the system handle this kind of problem at all? Does it fail quietly? Does it run out of time? Every answer created a new list of things to fix, and we had maybe a few weeks to work through that list. People were sleeping in the office. We were running evaluations overnight and reading the results at six in the morning.

Ken has spent his whole career around the Putnam, so he knows how brutal it is even for very strong students. I think he saw a small team trying to get a machine to that level on a fixed clock, with no option to say "we need another month," and that felt like a mobilization to him. There was no enemy, obviously. But there was this shared sense that the problem was bigger than any one of us, and the only way through was to work with a kind of intensity that you cannot sustain for long. I would not want to live that way permanently. For that stretch, though, it was the right thing.

r001.rationale: The response says the problems were released on Putnam morning and could not be prepared for, but does not say that morning’s paper contained more problems than expected across both sessions.

r002.rationale: It describes the team’s work and urgency without identifying near-exclusive reliance on Evan Chen or that reliance as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It contrasts taking time on a research lemma with working under the Putnam deadline, but does not distinguish the mathematical abilities research uses from those needed for competition problem-solving.

The Putnam is an individual exam, but preparing for it can be very collective: you struggle with problems together, share ideas, and push one another. “Wartime” captures that feeling of urgency and solidarity.
